science.title: Structure and functional divergence of the non-canonical BoNT-like toxin PG1 and PG2
science.description: Botulinum neurotoxins (BoNTs) are potent bacterial toxins. Distinct BoNT-like toxins, including BoNT/X, BoNT/En, and PMP1, form a distinct lineage. Here we characterize two additional members of this group, PG-toxin 1 and 2 (PG1 and PG2). Their light-chain (LC) and heavy-chain (HC) domains are encoded by adjacent genes. PG1 and PG2 LCs cleave Drosophila SNAP-25 at distinct sites (N196-E197 and R191-K193, respectively); PG1 is more potent, while PG2 activity depends on pH and ionic strength. Both LCs enter Sf9 cells via clathrin-mediated endocytosis. PG1 LC is toxic to Drosophila and northern armyworm independently of its HC, whereas PG2 LC toxicity is enhanced by its HC. Cryo-EM shows that PG1 adopts a distinct compact di-chain architecture with a door-hinge-like “belt.” These findings expand the structural and functional diversity of the BoNT family and support the potential of PG-toxins as insecticidal agents and research tools. Here the authors characterise two botulinum-like toxins, PG1 and PG2. Their light chains cut a key protein in fruit flies; PG1 is toxic even without its heavy chain. PG1 has a distinct compact structure. These findings expand toxin knowledge and suggest potential as insecticides or research tools.

science.title: Transport evidence for the orbital Nernst effect
science.description: Orbital Hall effects have recently attracted significant attention for generating substantial orbital angular momentum currents in both strong- and weak-spin-orbit-coupling materials. Despite extensive theoretical and experimental progress on the orbital Hall effect, its thermal counterpart, in which a temperature gradient drives a transverse orbital current, known as the orbital Nernst effect, has remained experimentally elusive. Here, we report the first experimental evidence for the orbital Nernst effect by measuring the magneto-thermopower in the yttrium iron garnet (YIG)/Pt/CuOx heterostructures. Through systematic comparison with the YIG/Pt and YIG/CuOx heterostructures, we show that both the magneto-thermopower and the magnetoresistance for YIG/Pt/CuOx are markedly enhanced due to the contributions from the orbital Nernst effect and the orbital Hall effect in CuOx, respectively. Our experimental evidence for the orbital Nernst effect supports the orbital degree of freedom as a promising route for heat-energy harvesting and orbital angular momentum thermal transport in earth-abundant materials. The authors report experimental evidence of the orbital Nernst effect, demonstrating that heat can generate transverse orbital currents in a copper oxide film and opening new opportunities for heat-driven orbitronics.

science.title: Comparative evaluation of fractal analysis and canny edge-detection algorithms for the quantification and classification of bone trabecular patterns in cone-beam computed tomography
science.description: While gray scale density metrics are susceptible to cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) noise and calibration inconsistencies, advanced image processing algorithms offer a potential non-invasive, objective alternative. This study presents a comparative evaluation of Fractal Analysis (FA) and Canny Edge-Detection (CED) algorithms for quantifying and classifying distinct bone trabecular patterns. In this ex vivo experimental study, 120 bovine rib bone blocks were categorized into four morphologic groups (D1-D4) and imaged using a standardized CBCT protocol. A single standardized 50 × 50-pixel region of interest (ROI) was analyzed on a selected two-dimensional reconstructed slice from each block. FA and CED quantified structural complexity and edge count, respectively. Group differences were evaluated using analysis of variance with multiplicity-adjusted post hoc tests, and exploratory receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were used to estimate pairwise discrimination. Both FA and CED values differed significantly across the four morphologic groups (p < 0.001). FA differentiated every pairwise comparison (p ≤ 0.014), whereas CED did not differentiate D2 from D3 (p = 0.717). Exploratory AUCs ranged from 0.77 to 0.99 for FA and from 0.64 to 1.00 for CED. Within this controlled ex vivo model, FA and CED provided objective, reproducible quantification of distinct trabecular bone patterns on CBCT images. FA excels in differentiating intermediate densities (D2 and D3), while CED offers superior performance for denser and looser bone patterns (D1 and D4). The complementary performance of the two algorithms supports their potential as quantitative adjuncts to visual bone-pattern assessment.
